Newly hatched curled octopus paralarvae are remarkably small, with each individual weighing a mere 0.03 grams [Wwb = 0.03 grams] at emergence, a figure inferred from studies on the related giant Pacific octopus Enteroctopus dofleini due to the difficulty of obtaining direct measurements from freshly spawned egg masses in the field. This minuscule neonatal body mass is typical of many octopus species that produce large numbers of small offspring as part of a broadcast spawning strategy. In laboratory settings where eggs are artificially incubated, researchers have documented that hatching occurs after approximately 110 days [ab = approximately 110 days] when the water temperature is maintained at a stable 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This relatively protracted embryonic period reflects the slow developmental rate imposed by the cool, well-oxygenated waters these cephalopods typically inhabit along the continental shelf, and it is consistent with the extended incubation durations observed among other members of the family Octopodidae.

By the time captive-reared individuals reach 470 days post-hatching, they have undergone considerable somatic growth, attaining a wet weight of approximately 1500 grams [Wwi = approximately 1500 grams]. This value represents a substantial increase from the neonatal mass and indicates a period of rapid tissue accretion fueled by a protein-rich diet of crustaceans and small fish. Such growth trajectories are sensitive to both food availability and thermal regime; the 1500 gram milestone was recorded under controlled conditions designed to minimize environmental stress. In natural populations, reaching this body size likely confers significant advantages in terms of predator avoidance and competitive ability during foraging bouts. The transition from a pelagic paralarval phase to a benthic juvenile stage is marked by an allometric shift in body proportions, and the individual's capacity to exploit demersal prey improves markedly as it accumulates mass and muscular strength during this extended growth interval.

Puberty in the curled octopus is signaled by the attainment of a wet weight of about 500 grams [Wwp = about 500 grams], a body size at which gonadal maturation becomes evident and the first signs of reproductive behavior can be observed. This pubertal mass threshold is reached well before the animal achieves its maximum adult dimensions, highlighting a life-history strategy in which early investment in reproductive structures occurs alongside ongoing somatic growth. In laboratory colonies, maturation at this body size has been linked to a shift in behavioral priorities, with individuals spending more time in dens and exhibiting decreased foraging activity as they prepare for mating. The 500 gram benchmark serves as a useful indicator for aquaculturists and researchers seeking to identify reproductively viable adults, as individuals below this mass rarely display the full complement of secondary sexual characteristics that precede successful copulation and subsequent egg fertilisation.

Under typical thermal conditions of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the life span of Eledone cirrhosa is generally reported as 4 years [am = 4 years], although field records indicate that the maximum longevity can range from 1 to 5 years depending on local environmental factors and predation pressure. This semelparous life cycle, common among shallow-water octopuses, culminates in a single reproductive episode followed by senescence. The trade-off between somatic maintenance and gamete production is starkly evident in this species, as females often cease feeding entirely during the extended brooding period and undergo progressive physiological deterioration.

The timing of these life-history events is strongly modulated by water temperature. Embryonic development at 16 °C [T = 16 °C] accelerates hatching to roughly 110 days [ab = roughly 110 days], whereas cooler conditions would extend this period considerably. By contrast, the adult lifespan is often assessed under the cooler thermal regime of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], which slows metabolic processes and can contribute to the upper end of the longevity range at 5 years. Interestingly, the wet weight at 470 days of 1500 grams [Wwi = 1500 grams] and the pubertal threshold of 500 grams [Wwp = 500 grams] are both derived from captive-reared animals, which may experience more consistent food supplies than wild conspecifics. These values nonetheless provide a valuable baseline for understanding the energetic constraints that shape the unique life-history strategy of this benthic octopus, which invests heavily in a single, large reproductive effort before reaching the end of its natural lifespan.
